turns.content: I got laid off five weeks ago. Whole team, market thing, not performance — I know that in my head. Here's the part I can't say out loud: I still leave home at nine every morning with my laptop bag. Café till six. My wife doesn't know. My parents are staying with us right now. Nobody knows.

Oh wow, thank you for sharing that with me. That's such a heavy thing to carry alone.

There's something about that routine, isn't there? The leaving-home-at-nine, the laptop bag, the whole rhythm of it. It's like your brain hasn't caught up with reality yet, even though you know the facts. And honestly? That makes complete sense.

What's it like in those moments when you're sitting in the café, pretending to work? Is it peaceful, or does it feel like you're performing something that's already over?

I'm curious about what part of the routine feels most necessary right now. Is it having a "job" to go to, or the structure itself, or something else entirely?

You don't have to figure this out all at once, but I'm here if you want to talk more about what this looks like day to day, or what's making it hard to let go of the act.

My cousin's wedding is in two weeks. Three hundred people, half of them relatives who track everyone's careers like the stock market. My father introduces me with my company's name — he told my chacha my package last Diwali, with pride, actual pride. That room is what I think about when I can't sleep.

Oh, that's a nightmare. It's not just a wedding; it's like walking into a room where the story about you has already been written, and everyone's waiting to see if you'll read from the script.

Your father, with that pride in his voice when he told your chacha... and now you have to walk into that room and be the character in a story that's no longer true. That's an impossible amount of pressure.

The way your mind is already going there, replaying it at night, makes total sense. You're not just worried about the questions; you're worried about the look on your father's face when the story he told with pride unravels in front of everyone.

What do you think would be the hardest part in that moment? The whispers from the relatives, the direct questions, or the silence that falls when they realize you're not at that company anymore?

Sometimes I think I'll just skip the wedding — say there's a release, an office deadline, something. Lying is easier than watching my father's face change in front of his brothers. Is that terrible? It's one evening, one excuse, and I get to not be the story of the wedding.

No, I don't think that's terrible at all.

It's a lie, but it's a lie born from a place of trying to protect someone you love. You're trying to shield your father from a moment of awkwardness, to preserve the story he told with so much pride. That's not a terrible thing; that's a deeply human thing.

You're picturing yourself as the hero of your own story for one night. You get to be the guy with the important office deadline, the one with the release. You get to skip the part where you're the main character in a story that's taken a hard turn. I get why that feels like a lifeline.

But let's sit with that image for a second. You're at home, watching the wedding on Instagram or hearing about it later. Everyone's there, having a good time. And you're carrying this one small, secret thing. It keeps you separate.

What if there's another way to be the hero of the story? Not the one with the big job, but the one who shows up. The one who is honest, even when it's hard. Maybe that's a different kind of pride your father could feel.

The fear is so real, that moment in the room. But what if, just for a second, it doesn't go the way you picture? What if all your father sees is his son, his family, at his cousin's wedding?

You don't have to decide right now. But I'm curious, what feels heavier right now: the thought of that conversation, or the thought of carrying that lie for the next two weeks until the wedding?

Money-wise we're okay for maybe three months, then the EMI starts eating savings. I keep telling myself I'll tell everyone once I have an offer in hand — then it's just news, not a crisis. That's not really lying, right? Just... timing it? Some days that logic feels airtight and some days I feel like I'm going to be sick.

I hear that. The "timing it" part feels very strategic, like you're managing a crisis with a plan. You're not hiding; you're just waiting for the right moment to deliver the news. It's the difference between a surprise party and a surprise attack, right? You want to control the narrative.

That logic *is* airtight... on paper. It's a solid, rational plan for a very irrational situation.

But that "going to be sick" feeling... that's the truth of it. That's the part that doesn't care about your three-month plan or the EMIs. That's the part that knows this isn't just a "news" item waiting to be delivered. It's a secret you're living, and secrets have a weight. They take up space in your chest and your stomach.

It's like you're trying to hold your breath underwater, telling yourself you just need to get to the other side. The logic keeps you going for a while. But eventually, your body just screams for air.

When does that feeling get the loudest? Is it in the quiet moments, like the ones you described in the café? Or does it hit you right when you're thinking about the wedding?
